1511a5759851a3e8.title: Afghan deportation plans raise fears for Christian evacuees

USA (MNN) — Court orders have temporarily protected some Afghans from deportation, but the fate of Afghan refugees in the United States remains uncertain.

Judges temporarily blocked some individual deportations amid reports of plans to remove about 150 Afghan nationals from the U.S. Advocates began raising alarms at the end of October when documents revealed administration plans to deport Afghans as part of a wider crackdown on illegal immigration.

90623669584cb433.title: Sweeping Anti-Conversion Law Leads Indian Churches to Cancel Vacation Bible Schools
90623669584cb433.summary:
Churches in the Indian state of Maharashtra are reportedly cancelling Bible camps during Diwali, a Hindu holiday celebrated during the autumn season, because of a recently enacted anti-conversion law.

For context, Maharashtra is India’s second most-populous state and includes Mumbai, the largest city in the country. Only about 2.3% of India’s 28 million people identify as Christians, making believers an extreme minority in the nation.

Much like in the U.S., the Bible camps — vacation Bible schools — last several days and consist of music, games and competitions, and stories and lessons based on Scripture, all for children ranging in ages from five to 15 years old. In India, they typically take place in the fall, according to Premier Christian News.

Some area churches, though, have cancelled their planned VBS events altogether, while others have restricted it strictly to Christian kids — a shift from the typical strategy of using the Bible camps as opportunities to evangelize.

It all comes down to Maharashtra’s sweeping Freedom of Religion Act, signed into law by Indian President Droupadi Murmu on July 30 and enacted the following month. The language of the bill is so broad, critics are concerned it will result in the penalization of Christians and churches. The law states violators may face up to seven years in prison for the non-bailable offense.

The new law bans conversion by “allurement,” a vague and overly generalized term that includes “any temptation in the form of … any gift, gratification, easy money or material benefit either in cash or kind.” It also disallows the offer of employment, “free education in school or college run by any religious body or institution,” a “better lifestyle,” “portraying practice, rituals and ceremonies or, any integral part of a religion in a detrimental way vis-a-vis another religion,” or even “glorifying one religion” — in this case, Christianity — over another.

Additionally, anyone who intends to convert from one religion to another is required to give notice to a governmental authority 60 days prior “to such proposed conversion.” At that point, the official will announce the impending conversion to the involved parties, “calling for objections within [30] days from issuance of notice,” according to the law.

“If any objections are received or otherwise, the competent authority [government official] may make an enquiry through police with regard to the intention, purpose or cause of the proposed conversion,” the bill states, noting that, if a violation is suspected, an investigation will ensue.

According to Premier, at least 12 other states in India have similar anti-conversion laws and, while advocates argue the bills protect vulnerable people from exploitation, others see them as a clear attack on Christian evangelism. The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, for example, has said the laws disproportionately affect Christians and Muslims, and have noted terms like “allurement” are intentionally ambiguous and problematic.

The churches moving ahead with planned VBS initiatives are requiring registration and charging entree fees of 50 to 100 rupees (roughly $1) as a way to prove parents sent their children to these faith-based camps intentionally and of their own accord.

74dd1a142c0b092c.title: Scholar Reveals New Josephus Analysis, Insight for Jesus’ Miracles and Resurrection
74dd1a142c0b092c.summary:
A college professor is revealing research he says helps corroborate early, extrabiblical writings about Jesus.

Dr. Thomas C Schmidt, associate professor of religious studies at Fairfield University, recently released, “Josephus & Jesus: New Evidence for the One Called Christ,” a book he believes helps set the record straight on Flavius Josephus’ writings.

“Josephus is one of the most important sources we have on the New Testament because he mentions so many people that are discussed in the New Testament, folks like Herod the Great, Herodias, Pontius Pilate, Caiaphas, Herod Agrippa, John the Baptist,” Schmidt said of the Jewish historian. “He talks about all these people, and he also talks about Jesus.”

But the professor said Josephus’ Jesus passage is “very controversial,” because many scholars have questioned the authenticity of this particular portion of the writings.

“They’ve thought that Christians tampered with it later on,” he said. “They thought Josephus didn’t actually write this. Josephus is writing in the first century. He was born in Jerusalem, raised in Jerusalem. So if he does tell us about Jesus, it would be the earliest witness to Jesus outside of Christian writings, which should just make it extraordinarily valuable and interesting.”

Schmidt said the majority position among scholars in the 19th century was that Josephus didn’t write any of the words about Jesus attributed to him and that the text was “completely fraudulent.”

“But then this brilliant scholar who was translating Josephus’ works, he started noticing that there were just many phrases in this account of Jesus that are odd phrases, but that Josephus himself uses many times elsewhere,” he said. “The scholar’s name was Henry Thackeray, and he turned the tide of arguments so that scholars started thinking, ‘Well, OK, clearly Josephus did say something about Jesus, but maybe Christians doctored it later on,’ because the belief by scholars was that what Josephus said was just too positive, too glowing to be written by a non-Christian.”

In the 21st century, scholars again looked at Josephus’ stylistic choices and found even more parallels between what was written about Jesus and Josephus’ other writings.

Schmidt conducted his own investigation for the book — and came to some fascinating conclusions.

“I exhaustively leverage these databases, and I show that every single phrase in the paragraph can be indexed back to Josephus in some way or another,” he said. “It sounds exactly like him. The turns of phrase, the vocabulary, everything sounds like Josephus.”

Schmidt said he also noticed something else in the passages some claim are “too pro-Christian.” One comment by Josephus is that Jesus worked miracles — something widely seen as supporting the Christian narrative. Schmidt said it’s more complex.

“Josephus says that Jesus worked miracles,” he said. “But the original Greek word is not quite so positive. It does mean ‘supernatural deeds’ but maybe we could better translate as ‘paranormal deeds.'”

Schmidt continued, “Josephus is acknowledging that Jesus worked supernatural deeds, but he’s unclear where the source of Jesus’ power is coming from. He doesn’t know if it’s malevolent, demonic — if it’s divine. In other words, Josephus looks like he’s assessing Jesus the same way the non-Christian Jews in the Gospels are responding to Jesus’s miracles.”

The academic said he started his journey writing “Josephus & Jesus: New Evidence for the One Called Christ,” on a quest to figure out how the Jesus passage had been changed by Christian scribes, adding that he initially agreed with the position that it wasn’t original.

“I was hoping that I could figure out what was changed so I could reconstruct what Josephus said,” he said. “But when I started looking at the results of these database searches, I became convinced that really the whole thing comes from Josephus.”

The resurrection is just one of the issues Schmidt addressed in his research.

“Traditionally, that part of the passage is translated as Josephus saying Jesus appeared alive again on the third day,” he said, noting that understanding the original language helps comprehension. “So, in other words, Josephus is not claiming that Jesus was resurrected. What he’s reporting is that the first disciples of Jesus claimed that Jesus was resurrected.”

And considering Josephus likely had access to people who put the disciples to death, he had remarkable first-hand information.

“Josephus didn’t just know people who knew the apostles; he knew people who knew Jesus, who were at his trial,” Schmidt said. “That’s the argument I make towards the end of my book. … I did not intend my book to be an argument in favor of Josephus’ passage being totally authentic, but that’s where the evidence led me.”

Spiritual warfare is a real part of the human experience, and the Bible explicitly details how events in the spiritual realm affect people.

“For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this dark world and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms,” Ephesians 6:12 (NIV) reads, with verse 13 continuing: “Therefore put on the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you may be able to stand your ground, and after you have done everything, to stand.”

The question isn’t if people will experience spiritual warfare; it’s when. A new survey from the American Bible Society (ABS) explores what Americans believe about spiritual warfare, specifically measuring how many people believe they have faced such attacks (watch CBN’s documentary “Investigating the Supernatural: Angels and Demons” today).

Dr. John Plake, editor-in-chief of the State of the Bible series and chief innovation officer at ABS, told CBN News that around 1-in-4 Americans report facing spiritual warfare.

“We saw real difference here across levels of faith participation,” he said. “About a fourth — 26% — of American adults say they’ve had that experience.”

He continued, “[Fifty-eight percent] of practicing Christians would agree with that statement, casual Christians, 28%, nominal Christians, 24%, and then non-Christians, 10%.”

The topic itself is quite fascinating, as Plake said it’s sometimes hard to quantify what a spiritual attack denotes. And since there’s not “a lot of deep data” there’s not qualitative information to help understand what respondents believe a spiritual attack looked like or entailed.

“I’m sure these people do have stories that they can tell about times when they felt like the negative experiences that they were having couldn’t be attributed just to natural causes, that there was some form of spiritual opposition that was going on,” Plake said. “And to see that incidence be that high, I was pretty fascinated by it.”

Another factor ABS was able to screen for was people’s reaction to a perceived spiritual attack — and those statistics were equally interesting.

“So 74% of people who [said they faced attack] said that the way they respond to spiritual attack is that they pray,” Plake said. “I think that makes a lot of sense, right? When spiritual attacks come, you may not be in a particular context where it’s easy to do much else, but you can always pray.”

The second-highest percentage was 36%, who said they declare Christ’s authority.

“There is this kind of sense that … they’re aware they’re in a spiritual battle, that their opposition isn’t … the person who may be opposing them at the moment,” Plake said. “But actually, there’s a spiritual thing going on here, and so they declare Christ’s authority.”

Next came the 24% who said they listen to praise and worship music, but then there’s the smallest — and most concerning — percentage: the 15% who said that they meditate on or quote Scripture.

“I would have hoped that would be a little bit higher,” Plake said. “And I think it also presents an opportunity for pastors and church leaders to recognize, ‘Hey, there are a lot of people, particularly in the church, who are having these experiences, and how can we equip them biblically to respond when they’re facing these kinds of spiritual attacks or moments of opposition, or even when there’s a need for a miraculous healing?'”

💼 Faith Driven Entrepreneur · A Structure for your Prayers
🌿 The True Vine · Day 1: The Vine
feed.html:
I am the True Vine--John 15:1


All earthly things are the shadows of heavenly realities--the expression, in created, visible forms, of the invisible glory of God. The Life and the Truth are in Heaven; on earth we have figures and shadows of the heavenly truths. When Jesus says: "I am the true Vine," He tells us that all the vines of earth are pictures and emblems of Himself. He is the divine reality, of which they are the created expression. They all point to Him, and preach Him, and reveal Him. If you would know Jesus, study the vine.
How many eyes have gazed on and admired a great vine with its beautiful fruit. Come and gaze on the heavenly Vine till your eye turns from all else to admire Him. How many, in a sunny clime, sit and rest under the shadow of a vine. Come and be still under the shadow of the true Vine, and rest under it from the heat of the day. What countless numbers rejoice in the fruit of the vine! Come, and take, and eat of the heavenly fruit of the true Vine, and let your soul say: "I sat under His shadow with great delight, and His fruit was sweet to my taste."
I am the true Vine.--This is a heavenly mystery. The earthly vine can teach you much about this Vine of Heaven. Many interesting and beautiful points of comparison suggest themselves, and help us to get conceptions of what Christ meant. But such thoughts do not teach us to know what the heavenly Vine really is, in its cooling shade, and its life-giving fruit. The experience of this is part of the hidden mystery, which none but Jesus Himself, by His Holy Spirit, can unfold and impart.
I am the true Vine.--The vine is the living Lord, who Himself speaks, and gives, and works all that He has for us. If you would know the meaning and power of that word, do not think to find it by thought or study; these may help to show you what you must get from Him to awaken desire and hope and prayer, but they cannot show you the Vine. Jesus alone can reveal Himself. He gives His Holy Spirit to open the eyes to gaze upon Himself, to open the heart to receive Himself. He must Himself speak the word to you and me.
I am the true Vine.--And what am I to do, if I want the mystery, in all its heavenly beauty and blessing, opened up to me? With what you already know of the parable, bow down and be still, worship and wait, until the divine Word enters your heart, and you feel His holy presence with you, and in you. The overshadowing of His holy love will give you the perfect calm and rest of knowing that the Vine will do all.
I am the true Vine.--He who speaks is God, in His infinite power able to enter into us. He is man, one with us. He is the crucified One, who won a perfect righteousness and a divine life for us through His death. He is the glorified One, who from the throne gives His Spirit to make His presence real and true. He speaks--oh, listen, not to His words only, but to Himself, as He whispers secretly day by day: "I am the true Vine! All that the Vine can ever be to its branch, "I will be to you."
Holy Lord Jesus, the heavenly Vine of God's own planting, I beseech Thee, reveal Thyself to my soul. Let the Holy Spirit, not only in thought, but in experience, give me to know all that Thou, the Son of God, art to me as the true Vine.

Andrew Murray, The True Vine (1898), day 1 of 31. Public domain. Source
